Here the register prints the forename in full, Francis, which is the word Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print; the abbreviation is on the town's side of this pair, not the register's.

UPHELD on a forename too odd to be a coincidence of initials, printed on both sides. The card reads S. Foot because the Democrat prints '§. FOOT' and Norris 1844 'Foot, S. teamster' — but Fergus 1839 and 1843 print the word itself: 'Foot, Star, teamster' and 'Foot, Starr, teamster, 180 Clark, cor Monroe'. The register's STAN is a fifth reading of Star/Starr, one letter apart in a transcription-mediated deposit, and not a fourth Christian name beginning with S. That is a token beyond the bare initial and it is what carries the ruling. The register's own arrangement agrees: the two Foots it holds, FOOT JOHN and FOOT STAN, take four consecutive lots of block 117 on one day, 22 October 1833 — John lots 5 and 6, Stan lots 3 and 4 — and the residents layer independently holds exactly two Foots, John and this one. THE LATER DIRECTORIES ARE USED HERE FOR THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE: 'teamster' is a trade of 1839 and is not back-projected onto 1835, and the card's 1835 trade stays the paper's.

REFUSED against C Goodrich. The town's whole record of that person is one line of the 1833 tax list — an initial and a surname, no trade, no street, no second document, no directory entry in 1839, 1843 or 1844 — and the card says so itself: a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else, the weakest rung of the ratified ladder. The register prints CHAUNCEY, a forename the town has never seen, and there is nothing on the town's side for it to be checked against. The mechanical rule reached this card because the initial C picked it out of the three Goodriches the layer holds, which is a fact about the layer and not about the man. That both records put a Goodrich at Chicago in 1833 does not close the gap: the school-section sale of October 1833 and the tax list of the same year are the two places a Chicago Goodrich would appear whether or not he is the same Goodrich. Four rows are retracted — lot 4 of block 48 and blocks 130, 131 and 132, $489 of ground.

UPHELD, and the register settles it without leaving the deposit. The same register prints HADDOCK EDWARD H twice — ls0172, lot 7 of block 120, 25 October 1833, three days after the E H rows and inside the same school-section sale, and ls0669 in the country in 1835 — so the abbreviation and the full forename are one hand at one sale. The middle initial H stands on both sides: the town prints 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st' in Fergus 1839 and John Wentworth's old-settler roll in the Tribune of 25 April 1882 carries 'Edward H. Haddock'. The card is the layer's strongest kind — seven sources, Andreas, the 1840 census, the Democrat — and the layer's only other Haddock is an H Haddock the forename refuses. Nothing here regrades the card or asserts a residence: it was already a documented townsman, and what the ruling adds is that these three rows are his.

UPHELD on the middle initial, which a contemporary Chicago paper prints and the register repeats. The Democrat of 31 December 1833, column 2, names him 'J. W. REED.' and gives his trade as cabinet maker — that is the town's own record, not a later directory — and the register prints REED JAMES W. Two tokens agree, not one: the W refuses George, Thomas and William Reed, and the forename refuses S W Reed, who is the only other Reed in the layer carrying a W. The register's other Reeds are ROBERT and THOMAS, and it never spells this purchaser any other way. The three lots are one day, 25 October 1833, inside the school-section sale. The household this person sits on is a reconstructed roof raised by the occupation census and this ruling does not touch it: it rules on the man, not the dwelling.

UPHELD, and like Haddock the register expands its own abbreviation: WRIGHT TRUMAN G appears twice in the same deposit, ls0518 and ls0566, both 27 June 1835 in T40N R14E. The middle initial G is on both sides — the card reads Truman G Wright off the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834, a letter list and the old-settler death notices — and it is what refuses the five other Wrights the layer holds, of whom three are Johns. The trade agrees in the strongest way this domain allows: Fergus 1839 prints 'Wright, Truman G., speculator, bds Tremont House', and six lots and blocks taken in block 70 and around it over three days of the October 1833 school-section sale — $1,282 of town ground in one week — is a speculator at work and not a householder buying somewhere to live. The word speculator is 1839's and is not written onto the 1835 card; it is used here to check an identity, which is what this file is for.

UPHELD on the initials as the town itself prints them, and on a date only one Beaubien can reach. The town's record of this man does not hold a forename it has to have expanded for it: Andreas's 1833 roster prints 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' and Fergus 1839 prints 'Beaubien, John B., Michigan ave., bet. Lake and So. Water sts' — J. B. is the form the town used, and the register's BEAUBIEN J B is that form. The layer holds ten Beaubiens and the sale is dated 29 September 1830: this card's arrival is attested at 1812 from Andreas — 'he came to Chicago and bought the cabin and cultivated field south of the old fort in 1812' — and it is the only Beaubien in the layer the record puts at Chicago that early. Four canal rows in section 29 of T39N R14E, two of them the register's own voided duplicates of the other two, carried at 212.61 acres and $1,063.20 net. TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not touch the Fort Dearborn reservation claim, which this project holds no record of and makes no finding on, and it does not make the 1830 purchase evidence of residence — the Residence column reads ILLINOIS on the voided pair and UNKNOWN on the pair that stood, and neither names a town.

REFUSED against L W Smith, on the same ground as SPENCER WILLIAM G under T-0700. The town's whole record of L W Smith is one line of the poll of 1834 — the card calls itself a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in any of the three directories. The register offers LIMAN, and the very next row, ls0573, offers SIMAN for the same tract on the same day at a price one cent apart: the deposit itself does not know whether the man was a Lyman or a Simon, so the token the mechanical rule matched on is not stable in the source that supplies it. The register's row carries no middle initial at all, so the W — the one token that could discriminate among the eleven Smiths the layer holds — is checked against nothing. The COOK in the Residence column sits on the SIMAN reading, not this one, and Cook County in 1834 reaches far beyond the town. One row retracted, 140.18 acres in T38N R14E section 2.

UPHELD, and this is the cleanest in the cohort: the register's forename is the town's own printed forename. Fergus 1843 has 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker, Jerome Beecher, res Market', and the register prints MONTGOMERY LOTON WM and MONTGOMERY LOTON W — Loton is not a name the deposit could have arrived at from an initial. The 1835 card itself rests on the Democrat, which prints 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' in five issues between 17 December 1833 and 20 May 1835 and gives the trade as boot and shoe maker, so the middle initial W is contemporary and not borrowed from 1843. The layer's only other Montgomery is a W Montgomery the forename refuses, and the register's only other is a JOHN whose Residence reads MCLEAN. Eighty acres of the east half of the south-east quarter of section 22, T38N R14E, on 24 November 1835 — the land rush, well south of the town, and the ruling asserts nothing about where he lived.

UPHELD on the same ground as MONTGOMERY LOTON WM: Fergus 1843's 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker' is the register's forename printed by the town, and the Democrat carries L. W. Montgomery through five issues of 1833–1835 with the trade. This is the earlier of his two entries — the north-west quarter of section 23, T38N R14E, 160 acres at $200 on 27 June 1835 — and it sits five months before and one section east of the other, which is one man buying twice in the rush rather than two readings of one sale.

REFUSED against T. M. Morrison, and refused on the rule's own named case. The town holds nothing but 'Morrison, T. M.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — no trade, no street, no household, no directory entry — and an uncalled-for letter says only that a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago. The M does appear on both sides, and that is the argument for upholding it; it does not carry, because the M is not a second reading of the man, it is one more character of the same single line, printed by the same list that supplies the T. The register adds THOS, which the town has never seen, and the layer holds five Morrisons — one of them Orsemus Morrison, a documented townsman who bought three town lots at the school-section sale, which is what a Morrison in this register looks like when the town really knows him. The ground here is a fractional quarter in T38N R15E section 32, the far south-east corner of the ring, 78.94 acres, and one row is retracted.

UPHELD, and the register proves it against itself. ls0919 — HUNTER E E, the north-east quarter of section 13, T40N R13E, 80 acres, $100, 15 November 1834 — and ls0920 — HUNTER EDWARD E, the same quarter of the same section on the same day at the same price — are one entry read twice, and the fuller reading states COOK in the Residence column where the abbreviated one leaves it UNKNOWN. So the expansion of E E to EDWARD E is the deposit's, not this ruling's, and it comes with the one column that speaks to residence. The middle initial E is on the town's side as well: the card is attested at G1b off the Democrat, the poll of 1834 and the old-settler death notices, and Fergus 1839 prints him as deputy-sheriff and ex-justice of the peace on Wells street. The layer's four other Hunters are refused on the forename. COOK is a county and not a town, and this ruling reads it as the register's word for the county, exactly as the domain's grading rule does.

NAMED, NOT UPHELD — the mechanical rule never proposed this one and could not. `namesake.choose` weighs the FIRST forename token, and the register prints this man's MIDDLE name in the forename's place, so GURTREY was put to all the Blanchards the town holds and named none of them. What names him is the town's own directory: Fergus 1843 prints 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells [died, Brooklyn, N.Y., 1872.]' — forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey — and Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print the same man 'Francis G.' GURTREY is that middle name, and the card carries it as Gantry because the poll of 1834 prints him 'Blanchard, F. Gantry'. THE REGISTER PROVES ITS OWN HABIT HERE, AT ONE SALE. The six GURTREY rows (purchase nos 0367525-0367530, volume 817 page 027) and the three F G rows (0376893-0376895, volume 818 page 010) are the SAME school section — section 16, T39N R14E, type SC — entered on 22 and 24 October 1833, the days the school section was sold off by lot and by block. One buyer, one auction, two volumes of the register, two renderings of one name; the domain's README already records this habit under T-0990, where HUNTER E E and HUNTER EDWARD E are the same 80 acres of section 13 on the same day at the same price. WHAT IS NOT NAMED BY IT. The town's other documented Blanchard is W. G. Blanchard, the house-and-land agent of the Democrat of 9 July 1834, and his forename initial is W: he is refused on the same ground the crosswalk refuses him against every other Blanchard reading. Joseph Blanchard the blacksmith is a man of the directories and not an 1835 resident. Nothing reached prints a second Gurtrey Blanchard anywhere. AND IT IS STILL A PURCHASE. The Residence column reads UNKNOWN on all six rows, so this names a buyer and never an occupant, and it places nobody on that ground. The six rows are lot 1 of block 2, block 21, lot 8 of block 141, block 3, lot 7 of block 82 and lot 1 of block 141 of the school section, $547.00 in all (ls0076-ls0081). Two of them state a price per acre of 3.69 against 0000.00 acres, which is the acreage of the F G row ls0074 standing in the wrong column of the deposit; it is carried as the register has it and read as no acreage at all.

UPHELD, on cohort A's discriminator: the town's card holds only initials — J. K. Botsford — and the directories print the forename whole. Fergus 1839 has 'Botsford, Jabez K., Botsford & Beers', Fergus 1843 'Botsford, Jabez Kent (B. & Beers), 109 Lake', Norris 1844 'Botsford, J. K. of B. & Beers'. The register writes JABEZ K, which is the 1839 line exactly, so the forename and the middle initial are both checked against a printing the town holds rather than against the initial the mechanical rule matched on. The card is attested at a TRADE besides — sheet iron worker, stove manufacturer, tinsmith, at the Democrat of 10 September 1834 — and a tinsmith with a shop taking two school-section blocks at the sale of 24 October 1833 is a townsman buying town ground. Nothing here says he lived on either block: what is carried is that he entered them.

UPHELD, and by the same route. The town's card is J. K. Boyer; Fergus 1839 prints 'Boyer, John K., coroner, South Water street near Clark', which supplies the forename AND repeats the middle initial, and the register writes JOHN K. The card is on the poll lists and in the Democrat as well, so the man is held at Chicago across the nine school-section lots of 22 and 25 October 1833 and the 80 acres of 13 June 1835. The 1839 trade is not read back onto 1835 — the card's own occupation stays none_recorded with the coronership in later_occupation, and this ruling does not touch it.

UPHELD. The middle initial is on both sides and the town's record is one of the densest it holds: Andreas's 1833 roster has 'George W. Dole, merchant', the Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries the forwarding and commission firm's own advertisement, and the directories print him George W. in 1839, George Washington in 1843 and Geo. W. in 1844. The register writes DOLE GEORGE W. He is the only George W. Dole in either record, he is documented in the town in the same season as the school-section sale of October 1833, and a forwarding merchant taking a block and two lots at that sale is the purchase the record would predict. The register's other Dole spelling, the bare DOLE, is a different reading and is not touched by this ruling.

UPHELD, and on the bracket rather than on an initial — the register gives no middle initial here, and this ruling does not pretend otherwise. What carries it is that the forename agrees IN FULL on a surname each record holds exactly once, and that the town holds Alexander N. Fullerton continuously across both entry dates in eight sources: Andreas counts him one of the six lawyers who had put out a sign by the close of 1833, which is the month of the school-section lots of 24 and 25 October 1833, and the American of 1835, the Democrat and the poll lists hold him through the summer of the ring entries of 26 June 1835. The directories then print him whole — Alex. N., Alexander Nathaniel, A. N. — on the same Dearborn street address. Both entry dates are bracketed by documents that put this man in this town; that is the rule's second limb and not a bare-name coincidence. No residence on any of the six parcels is asserted.

UPHELD. The register writes GOODHUE JOSIAH C and Fergus 1839 prints 'Goodhue, Dr. Josiah C., Dearborn street north of Lake street' — forename, middle initial and honorific, the same three tokens in the same order. The card is attested at a trade off the Democrat of 4 February 1834, physician, and is held again on the poll lists and in the old-settler death notices. One Goodhue in the register and one in the layer. The single lot — lot 4 of block 119, taken at the school-section sale of 25 October 1833 for $253 — is carried as an entry and not as a dwelling; the card's placement is unchanged.

UPHELD. The card carries the initial only, W. Kimball, and Fergus 1839 prints 'Kimball, Walter, probate judge, cor. Clark and South Water st' — the forename whole, at the corner the card already holds him at, because his own signed advertisement in the Democrat of 26 November 1833 opens a New Store for dry goods at the corner of South Water and Clark. The register writes WALTER. A merchant with a store at that corner taking lot 2 of block 49 at the school-section sale of 25 October 1833 is consistent with everything the town holds of him, and the Calumet Club and Tribune old-settler notices hold him after. The layer's other Kimball reading, Wm. Kimbal, disagrees on the forename and is not this man.

UPHELD, and the middle initial is on the TOWN's side, not only the register's: the card's press reading is 'E. S. Kimberley' in the Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, and the 1840 census reads 'Ed. Kimberley' — two independent documents bracketing the scene date, the earlier of them printing the S the register repeats when it writes KIMBERLEY EDMUND S. That is the NEWBERRY WALTER L check of T-0700 and not a bare name. RE-POINTED UNDER T-1001, AND THE MAN IS THE SAME MAN. T-0990 upheld this onto `kimberley_ed` and said in the same breath what the crosswalk could not see: the layer ALSO held `kimberly_edmund_s`, Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly — attested off Andreas, the poll lists and a history of medicine at Chicago, printed 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S.' in Fergus 1839 and 'Kimberly, Edmund Stoughten, physician, 101 Lake' in Fergus 1843 — the same forename and the same middle initial, spelled Kimberly rather than Kimberley, and never gathered as a rival because tools/namesake.py folds surnames exactly. T-1001 ruled that card question: the Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835 sets both spellings in one column of one page, and 'Dr. Kimberly' four sentences after 'E. S. Kimberley' inside one article, so the variation is the compositor's and is demonstrated rather than supposed. `kimberley_ed` is folded onto `kimberly_edmund_s` under C9 in data/residents/card_merge_rulings.json, and this ruling names the survivor. THE ENTRY IS NOT LOST TO A LETTER: with that card folded the residents layer holds no Kimberley at all, so the crosswalk's surname bucket now reaches this man through the landed card-merge adjudication (tools/read_land_sales.py `merged_card_surnames`, and the match carries `via_card_merge`). What is still refused is a mechanical fold of the surnames themselves — measured, and the count is in tools/measure_surname_fold.py. A purchase and nothing more, as before: it dates and places a transaction and proposes no residence.

amended.why: The card the ruling upheld the purchaser onto no longer stands on its own: T-1001 ruled `kimberley_ed` and `kimberly_edmund_s` one man and the merge landed, so the ruling is re-pointed at the survivor. Nothing about the JUDGEMENT changes — the same rows, the same reasoning, the same man — only the card id it names.

ruled.reasoning: UPHELD on the middle initial, which is the rule's first limb and is unusually safe here. The town's card is A V Knickerbacker off the poll lists, Norris 1844 prints 'Knickerbacker, A. V. grocery and provisions, South Water st', and the register writes ABRM V — the same middle initial V, with the forename expanded to a reading of Abraham the register supplies and the town does not. The surname is uncommon enough that the register holds it once and the layer holds it once, and the V agrees where a bare A would have decided nothing. Lot 1 of block 72 and block 101, entered 22 and 23 October 1833 at the school-section sale, are carried as entries. The 1844 grocery is not read back onto 1835 and the card's occupation is untouched.

UPHELD, on three initials rather than one. The register writes PECK P F W; the town holds Philip F. W. Peck off Andreas's 1833 roster — 'P. F. W. Peck, merchant' — and the directories print him Philip F. W. in 1839, Philip Ferdinand Wheeler in 1843 and P. F. W. in 1844. A three-initial string agreeing token for token is not a coincidence the bare-name rule has to worry about. He is a merchant with a two-storey store at South Water and LaSalle in the season of the school-section sale, and blocks 116 and 6 taken on 23 and 24 October 1833 are the purchase that record predicts. The register's other Peck, PECK EBENEZER, is a different man and is not touched. Nothing is asserted about where he lived.

UPHELD, on the forename and the trade together. The card is J. Shrigley, attested at a trade off the Democrat of 8 October 1834 — tavern keeper — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Shrigley, John, tavern keeper', which supplies the forename the register writes and repeats the trade the card already held. Fergus 1843 holds him still. One Shrigley in the register, one in the layer, and the town's own record independently attests both tokens the proposal turned on. The 80 acres in T40N R14E entered on 27 June 1835 are carried as an entry; a tavern keeper's premises are in the town and this ruling does not move them.

UPHELD. The card holds a trade attested off the Democrat of 13 August 1834, provision dealer, and the directories print both the forename and the continuation of that trade: Fergus 1843 'Marsh, Sylvester, 98 Lake, packing-house, 304-6 North Water', Norris 1844 the same. The register writes SYLVESTER, which is the directories' spelling rather than the card's Silvester, so the printing the ruling checks against is the one that agrees with the register letter for letter. A provision dealer who becomes a packer is the trade a man buying 160 acres in T38N R14E in June 1835 and two more eighties in February 1836 is buying ground for, and the surname is held once in each record. The card's occupation and its placement are untouched: what is carried is that he entered the parcels.

UPHELD, and this is the line the cohort's refusals are drawn against. The town holds L. T. Jamison TWICE and independently — the Democrat of 4 June 1834 and the poll of 1835, both graded G1a, both printing the same two initials — so the record brackets the scene date instead of resting on one reading. The register writes LOUIS T: it repeats the middle initial T, which is the rule's first limb, and expands the L to a forename the town has not seen. Where the same expansion appears in this cohort on a card that holds ONE name-only line, it has been refused; here the initial pair is attested on two documents of different kinds, one of them a poll list, which is the NEWBERRY WALTER L shape of T-0700. The two entries of December 1835 and January 1836 are carried as entries and assert no residence on either tract.

REFUSED against A. Chipman, on the SPENCER WILLIAM G ground of T-0700. The card is marked `letter_list_only`: the town's whole record of this person is one line of the Democrat's return of uncalled-for letters at 1 July 1835 — no trade, no street, no second document, no directory entry in 1839, 1843 or 1844 — and the household around them was written, in its own words, to claim nothing. The register supplies ANSEL, a forename the town has never seen, and the mechanical rule fired because the layer holds exactly one Chipman, which is a fact about how thin the layer is. THE RESIDENCE COLUMN WAS WEIGHED AND DOES NOT CARRY IT: ls0001 and its twin are one entry read twice, and the fuller reading states COOK. That is what upheld DILL FRANK in T-0700 — but there the town's side was a poll list, a document that says a man lived in the place, and here it is a letter somebody had not called for. A COOK entry and an uncalled-for letter are two name-only readings that agree about a county, and the rule refuses those however unlikely the coincidence looks. The 80 acres in section 4, T39N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against Edmund Roberts. The forename agrees in full, and nothing else does. The town's record is the 1833 tax list — 'Roberts, Edmund', graded G3 — and a Second Presbyterian retrospect of 1892: two name-only readings, no trade, no street, no middle initial, no directory line in any of the three volumes. The register's row carries no middle initial either, so there is no token for the town's side to be checked against. Two things make it worse rather than better. The entry is dated 5 OCTOBER 1830, three years before the earliest reading the town holds of this man, and nothing brackets that gap. And the surname is not rare in the source that supplies it: the same register sells to ROBERTS CHARLES and ROBERTS MARY, so the layer holding exactly one Roberts is a fact about the layer and not about Cook County. The 40 acres in section 9, T39N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against J Stanley, on the GOODRICH CHAUNCEY ground of cohort A. The town's whole record is one line of the 1833 tax list — 'Stanley, J.', graded G3, an initial and a surname — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. The register prints JOSEPH, a forename the town has never seen, and there is nothing on the town's side for it to be checked against. The mechanical rule reached this card because the initial J is the only Stanley the layer holds. That both records put a Stanley at Chicago in 1833 does not close the gap: the school-section sale of October 1833 and the tax list of the same year are the two places a Chicago Stanley would appear whether or not he is the same Stanley. Lot 4 of block 118, $131.50, is retracted.

REFUSED against Herman A. Rowley, and the agreeing middle initial is the reason this one needed saying. The card is `letter_list_only`: one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 20 May 1835, printing 'Rowley, Herman A.' — an initial pair and nothing else, no trade, no street, no second document, no directory line. The register writes HEMAN A, so the A does agree, and the forename differs by a letter that either hand could have made. A MIDDLE INITIAL DISCRIMINATES; IT DOES NOT CORROBORATE. In T-0700 the L of NEWBERRY WALTER L decided among candidates the town already held in the American of 1835 and both Fergus directories; here it is the whole of the town's record, and two name-only readings do not make an identity because one of them is fuller than the other. The 160 acres in section 6, T40N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against N F Hurd, on the same reading of the middle initial as ROWLEY HEMAN A above. The town's record is a single press line — 'N. F. Hurd' in the Democrat of 25 June 1834, graded G1b — with no trade, no street, no second document and no directory entry. The register writes NIRAM F: the F agrees and the forename is one the town has never seen, so the agreeing token is the same token the mechanical rule matched on and the expansion is checked against nothing. The register settles the other half of it directly — it also sells to HURD DENNIS S, so Cook County held at least two Hurds while the layer held one, and the uniqueness the rule leaned on is a property of the layer. The two parcels in section 30, T38N R15E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against Tho's Allison. The card is `letter_list_only`: a letter was still waiting for this name at the Democrat of 1 July 1835 and that is the entire record — no trade, no street, no second document, no directory line. The forename agrees, and agreement on a forename is what the mechanical rule already had. The Residence column states COOK on this row, which is the strongest thing the register offers and which upheld DILL FRANK and LUDBY JOHN; in both of those the town's side was a document of residence or a newspaper naming the man in the town between his entries, and here it is a letter nobody called for. A tract entry by a Cook County Thomas Allison in April 1835 and an uncalled-for letter addressed to a Chicago Thomas Allison in July are two name-only readings that agree about a county. The 160 acres in section 30, T40N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against J. L. Sackett. The card is `letter_list_only` — one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 2 July 1834, an initial pair and a surname, and the card's own note says the corpus stops before the scene date. The register writes SACKETT JOSHUA, which agrees with the J and carries NO middle initial at all, so the L — the one token that could have discriminated — is checked against nothing, and the forename Joshua is one the town has never seen. This is SPENCER WILLIAM G with the disagreement on the other side of the name. The 80 acres in section 32, T40N R14E, entered 30 May 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against Catherine Ostrander, and with some regret, because a woman entering 79.46 acres in her own name in May 1835 is worth more than the record can carry. The card is `letter_list_only`: one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 22 October 1834, no trade, no street, no second document, and the card's own present_on_scene_date reads `uncertain` because nothing follows her to 1 July 1835. The forename agrees; the register's F in the social-status column confirms the register's own reading of its own row and says nothing about the town's. Two name-only readings. The parcel in section 4, T38N R14E is retracted, and the register's entry stands on its own as a woman's purchase in Cook County — it is the identification with the town's Catherine Ostrander that is refused, not the purchase.

REFUSED against B Blaisdell. The town's whole record is one line of the poll of 1835 — 'Blaisdell, B.', graded G2a — with no trade, no street, no second document and no directory entry, and the card's arrival bound falls AFTER the scene date, so even the town's one reading does not place him there on 1 July 1835. The register prints BENJAMIN, a forename the town has never seen, checked against an initial. That is the GOODRICH CHAUNCEY shape exactly. The 160 acres in section 24, T38N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against A. Shepherd. The card is `letter_list_only` — the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 2 July 1834, one line, no trade, no street, no second document, nothing following him to the scene date. The register prints ALBERT against the town's bare A. The layer holding one Shepherd is what fired the rule and is a fact about the layer. The 80 acres in section 32, T38N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against D Wilcox. The town's record is one press line — 'Capt. D. Wilcox' in the Democrat of 4 February 1834, graded G1b — and the honorific is a rank, not a check: the register's social-status column is blank on all three of these rows, so there is nothing on its side for a captaincy to agree with. What the register does print is DE LA FAYETTE, as distinctive a forename as this cohort contains and one the town has never seen, reduced by the mechanical rule to the initial D. A striking name checked against a single letter is the weakest reading the rule admits, not the strongest. The three parcels in sections 32, 33 and 34 of T38N R14E, entered between December 1835 and March 1836, are retracted.

REFUSED against Thomas Church, and not because the man is a stranger — the directories hold him firmly enough, a grocer at 109-111 Lake through 1839, 1843 and 1844. Two things refuse it. The register writes THOS JR, and the JR is the page saying there was ANOTHER Thomas Church of the same county, presumably the father; the town holds one Thomas Church and nothing on its side distinguishes the two, so the one token that discriminates here is checked against nothing. And the town's 1835 record of him is thinner than the directories make it look: the card is written, in its own words, almost entirely to keep a building from being anonymous, its present_on_scene_date says nothing places him in the town on any particular date, and the source that names him names him as the BUILDER of the first store on Lake Street rather than as its occupant. That the identification is probably right is not what is refused. The 160 acres in section 34, T39N R13E, entered 5 August 1835, are retracted.

The town holds this man twice and neither reading is the tract entry. The Chicago Democrat prints 'Wm. Andrews' at Chicago on 25 June 1834, and Fergus's directory of 1839 prints 'Andrews, William, tailor, north side' — a contemporary printing and a directory line four years later, both on the north side of a town of four thousand. What makes the pair worth more than its two bare names is that the REGISTER agrees with the layer on the shape of the family: it sells to an ANDREWS WILLIAM and, separately, to an ANDREWS DAVID, and Fergus prints a William Andrews and a David Andrews as tailors on the same side of the river. The proposal is upheld on the second document, which is the rule's own third arm; the register's single row and its UNKNOWN Residence column add nothing and the reasoning does not lean on them.

The middle initial is on both sides and it is not the whole of the case. The Chicago American names William B. Archer at Chicago on 4 July 1835 — three days after the scene date and inside the window this project reads — and Fergus's roll of old settlers' deaths carries him again. The layer's only rival is a Joseph Archer, so the initial had one alternative to beat and beat it; two documents naming the man in full are what carries the ruling. A canal commissioner entering Illinois ground in 1835 is the purchase the record would predict rather than one it has to accommodate.

Ten Beaubiens stand in the layer and exactly one is a Mark. He is the most heavily documented of them: the incorporation election of 10 August 1833 was held at his house by the clerk's printed notice, he voted for incorporation on 5 August, he is on the 1833-1835 voter lists, Fergus 1839 prints 'Beaubien, Mark, hotel-keeper, Lake st' and Fergus 1843 prints him again as the light-house keeper on River street. Five independent documents, and the forename is the discriminator the register's own spelling supplies. The two tract rows are upheld against the man who kept the Sauganash.

This is the shape cohort B named and could not always find: the Residence column WITH a town-side partner. One of the four rows states COOK, and the town's partner is the poll list of 1834 — a civic document of the place, not a name a correspondent posted a letter to. Fergus 1839 then prints 'Bennett, William, soap boiler'. A man polled at Chicago in 1834 and trading there in 1839, against a purchaser the register itself seats in Cook County, is two records agreeing on more than a name. The card's own grade stays where it is: a ruling never raises one.

Four documents on the town's side, all of them before or around the purchase: the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834, the Calumet Club's roll of early Chicago, and Fergus 1839 printing 'Bowen, Erastus, city collector, So. Water st, cor. Michigan ave.' A town collector of that name is continuously in the record from 1833, and the register sells one tract to an ERASTUS BOWEN. Upheld on the second, third and fourth documents. THE CAVEAT IS WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN BURIED: Fergus 1843 prints TWO men of this name — 'Bowen, Erastus (B. & Cole), res 40 Michigan ave' and 'Bowen, Erastus Selden [veterinary surgeon] [died Oct. 19, 1888, a. 69]' — and the second, aged 69 at his death in 1888, was born about 1819 and was sixteen in 1835. The purchaser is the elder, who is also the man the 1833 tax list and the 1839 directory carry; the card this proposal lands on is keyed `bowen_erastus_selden` and appears to have gathered both. That is a conflation on the CARD, not a fault in the match, and it is filed as its own ticket rather than settled inside a ruling.

Every arm of the rule fires at once. The middle initial is printed on both sides; the Chicago Democrat names 'W. H. Brown' at Chicago on 28 May 1834 and 'Wm. H. Brown' a week later; Fergus 1839 prints 'Brown, William H., cashier, Branch State Bank Illinois, LaSalle st cor. So. Water'; and one of the two register rows states ILLINOIS in its Residence column. The cashier of the branch bank is exactly the sort of man these rows are full of. Upheld — and note that this is the FULL spelling; the register's bare BROWN WM is ruled separately and does not go the same way.

The best-documented proposal in the cohort, and the one where the purchase is what the record predicts rather than merely permits. Philo Carpenter is one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833, an original elder of the First Presbyterian Church, an advertiser in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, and 'Carpenter, Philo, druggist and apothecary, South Water st' in Fergus 1839. By 1843 both Fergus and Norris seat him in CARPENTER'S ADDITION — a subdivision carrying his own name, which is to say the man platted and sold Chicago ground. Three tract entries against him are the beginning of that, not a coincidence of surname. The two other Carpenters in the layer are an Abel B. and a Nathaniel and neither is reachable from the register's forename.

The card is flagged `letter_list_only` and the flag is WRONG, which is why this proposal does not go the way cohort B's letter-list refusals went. Of the four press readings on the record only ONE is a letter list (the Democrat's return of 1 April 1834); the other three are ordinary printings — the Democrat of 26 November 1833, the Chicago American of 24 December 1833, the Democrat of 13 August 1834 — each with its own locator. So the town holds this man printed by name three times outside the post office, with the middle initial the register repeats, and Fergus 1839 prints 'Chapman, Charles H., real estate dealer, Randolph street'. A real-estate dealer entering three tracts is the fourth arm of the rule as well as the third. Upheld. The stale flag is filed as its own ticket — six other cards carry it the same way.

Four Clarks stand in the layer, two of them Johns, and the middle initial is what separates John K. from John A. — the register prints K and the card prints K. On its own that would only discriminate, not corroborate, which is cohort B's warning. What corroborates is the Chicago American of 11 July 1835 printing 'John K. Clark' at Chicago in full, ten days after the scene date, and one of the three register rows stating COOK in its Residence column. A man named in the town's own paper inside the window, seated in Cook County by the register, with the middle initial agreeing on both sides.

Cohort A's lesson, exactly: where the town's card holds an initial, look for the volume that prints the name whole. Norris 1844 prints 'Cook, Josiah P. baker, res Michigan avenue' — forename, middle initial, trade and street together — and the register's purchaser is COOK JOSIAH P. Five Cooks stand in the layer and the middle initial refuses the nearest of them, a J. B. Cook. The town's second document is the tax list of 1833, which places a Cook of this household here two years before the entry. Josiah P. Cook is not a name that turns up twice by accident in a town this size.

A common name carried by an uncommonly stable record. The town holds Thomas Cook in the tax list of 1833, in the 1840 census, and in three directories that agree with one another on the trade AND the street: 'teamster, Desplaines st near Monroe' in 1839, 'teamster, Desplaines. south of Randolph' in 1843, 'teamster, Desplaines st' in 1844, with a death notice at Western Springs in 1885 aged 85. That is one man in one place for a decade, not a name recurring. The two tract rows are upheld against him on the second-document arm; the register's UNKNOWN Residence column carries nothing and the ruling does not pretend otherwise, and a teamster is not a trade the purchase would have predicted.

Two name-only readings, and the commonest name pair in the cohort. The town's whole 1835 record of this person is ONE return of uncalled-for letters — 'Allen, William', Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — and the card carries `letter_list_only`, which cohort B found is this test written as a field. The register offers a single row with an UNKNOWN Residence column and no middle initial. The later Fergus and Norris lines ('Allen, Wm., shipcarpenter') reach this card by the same surname fold that is under question and cannot corroborate it. A correspondent believing a William Allen reachable at Chicago and a William Allen entering ground do not make one man. The paragraph the spend pass wrote is retracted.

The card is `letter_list_only` and the one return is the Democrat's of 1 July 1835, printing 'Andrews, Davi' — a truncation the layer has kept as the person's name. The research row attached to it is graded `corroborated_enrichment` with an EMPTY evidence_for field, so nothing in it can be checked against a tract entry. Two rows in the register, UNKNOWN Residence, no middle initial, no trade. Its sibling ANDREWS WILLIAM is upheld above and this one is not, and the difference is the whole rule: that card carries a newspaper printing and a directory trade, this one carries a letter waiting at the post office. Refused; the spend pass's paragraph is retracted.

The 1835 poll list ALONE — the card's own grade, G2a, says so — and one tract row with an UNKNOWN Residence column. A poll list is a better document than a letter list and it is still one name-only reading; the town holds nothing else about this man, no trade, no street, no directory line in 1839, 1843 or 1844, and no second printing. The rule refuses a bare name on each side however unlikely the coincidence looks, and Thomas Ballard is not an unlikely name.

`letter_list_only`, and both press readings are the same kind of thing: 'Bleke, Levi' in the Democrat's return of 20 May 1835 and 'Blake, Levi' in the return of 19 August 1835 — two letters waiting at the same post office, one of them printed under a mangled surname. No directory prints him in 1839, 1843 or 1844. One tract row, UNKNOWN Residence. Cohort B's finding applies without softening: repeating the weakest evidence does not strengthen it. Refused, and the spend pass's paragraph is retracted.

The counter-example to cohort A's habit, and the reason that habit is a HABIT and not a rule. The register does print the same purchaser twice under two spellings often enough — but BROWN WM carries no middle initial, and the layer's only William Brown happens to be William H. because the layer is THIN, not because the town had one. It did not: Fergus 1843 prints three distinct men — 'Brown, William, grocer, res N. Water', 'Brown, Wm., bds Sauganash [died, Nevada City, Cal., Dec. 3, 1850]' and 'Brown, William Hubbard, [cashier]' — and Norris 1844 prints the first two again. A bare Wm. Brown on a tract row could be any of them or a fourth. The FULL spelling BROWN WILLIAM H is upheld above on its middle initial and its bank; these two rows are refused, and what the spend pass carried from them comes back off the card.

An uncommon name and it changes nothing — the rule refuses a bare name on each side however unlikely the coincidence looks, because the unlikeliness is a feeling and the record is what is being checked. The card is `letter_list_only` at G3, a projected resident: 'Burdick, Paul' in one return of uncalled-for letters, Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, and the card's own note says nothing else in the corpus names him — no trade, no street, no household, no arrival. No directory row in any of the three volumes. Two register rows, UNKNOWN Residence. Refused.

The COOK THOMAS pattern on the commonest surname in the block: a common name carried by an uncommonly stable record. The register itself sells to six Davises and discriminates them by forename, and the town holds George Davis five times over a decade with the forename printed WHOLE every time — the poll of 1834, the 1840 census head 'Geo Davis', and three directories that agree with one another on the office and the street: 'Davis, George, county clerk, 109 Lake st' in 1839, 'clerk, county commiss'rs' court … 107 Lake, res Canal near W. Washington' in 1843, the same office and the same house in Norris 1844. That is one man in one post for ten years, not a name recurring, and the poll of 1834 stands between the two register rows of 27 June 1835 and 8 January 1836. Upheld on the rule's second-document arm; the eighteen acres are carried as an entry, the Residence column reads UNKNOWN and this ruling does not lean on it, and a county clerk is not a trade the purchase would have predicted.

The block's BROWN WM, and the card says so itself before any ruling does. John Davis is one of the commonest names the register holds; the four rows of 22 and 24 October 1833 print it bare, with no middle initial and UNKNOWN in the Residence column. The town's card is a HOTEL KEEPER attested in the American of 1835, and all three directories print a different trade at a fixed address — 'Davis, John, tailor, North Water street, near Kinzie' in 1839, 'tailor' again in 1843, 'sailor, North Water st.' in Norris 1844 — so the printed record of a John Davis at Chicago is not the man the card asserts. The card's own note already refuses to resolve the coincidence: 'a ‘Mr. Davis’ also took over the Sauganash Hotel in 1835, and whether that is this man is unknown … if it is not, there is a second Davis in the town.' A bare forename on a surname the town's own record doubles cannot be assigned to either of them. Refused, and what the spend pass carried from these four rows comes back off the card.

The strongest proposal in the cohort, and it satisfies three of the rule's four arms at once. The MIDDLE INITIAL is on both sides and the town prints the middle name in full besides: the tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1834 print 'Egan, William Bradshaw', Fergus 1843 'Egan, Wm. Bradshaw', Norris 1844 'Egan, Wm. B.' The TRADE is what the purchase would predict — Fergus 1839 prints 'Egan, Dr. William B., REAL ESTATE DEALER, bds. City Hotel', and Andreas has him buying the Tremont House block from General Beaubien and building the five houses known as Egan's Row, which is why a physician is also one of the town's builders. The register enters him six times between 3 September 1835 and 1 January 1836 for 720 acres at $900, which is that dealer at work. He is the ONLY Egan the register holds and the only adult Egan of the surname the layer holds. Upheld.

Upheld on the second-document arm, with the register's own family shape agreeing. The town holds John Foot on two contemporary civic rolls that BRACKET the entry — the tax list of 1833, the same year as the two school-section rows of 22 October 1833, and the poll of 1835 after it — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Foot, John I[.], blacksmith, Randolph street, near State', which supplies a trade and a street the register never had. What makes the pair worth more than two bare names is the ANDREWS WILLIAM test: the register sells to a FOOT JOHN and, separately, to a FOOT STAN, and the layer holds a John Foot and an S. Foot — the two records agree on the shape of the surname, and cohort A upheld FOOT STAN as Starr Foot on the same page of reasoning. A blacksmith taking two town lots at the school-section sale for $190 is consistent with everything the town holds of him.

The town elected this man to office ten months after the entry, and the entry is ground inside the town. The Chicago Democrat of 13 August 1834 reports that 'Messrs. John H. Kinzie, G[ordon S. Hub]bard, J. K. Boyer, Ebenezer G[oodrich and J.] S. C. Hogan, were elected Trustees of this Town, for the term of one year' — a named Chicago TOWN TRUSTEE, not a name in a list — and the poll of 1834 holds him independently. The register's single row is lot 1 of block 93 of the school section, bought at the town's own sale of 22 October 1833 for $100: a trustee-to-be buying a town lot at the town's sale. The forename is uncommon and printed in full on both sides, and the layer holds exactly one Ebenezer Goodrich where the register holds three Goodriches it discriminates by forename. Cohort A refused GOODRICH CHAUNCEY, which is a different question: there the town held no Chauncey at all and an initial chose.

The full spelling of a purchaser cohort A already upheld abbreviated, and the PEARSONS reasoning applies unchanged: upholding HADDOCK E H and refusing HADDOCK EDWARD H would be incoherent, since the abbreviated spelling was upheld precisely because the town prints the forename whole. The MIDDLE INITIAL H is on both sides and Fergus 1839 prints it out — 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st'. The town holds him five times besides: the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834 ('Haddock, Edward E.', the same man's forename whole), the poll of 1835, three printings in the Democrat of 1834, and the 1840 census. The tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1835 bracket both rows, 25 October 1833 and 27 June 1835. A commission merchant taking eighty acres at the ring is consistent with the trade the card holds.

The town's whole record of George Hall is that somebody else repudiated a note owed to him. The Chicago Democrat of 29 July 1835 prints a caution 'against purchasing a Note, given by me to George Hall, dated June 24. 1835, for fifty dollars' — and the advertiser's own name is sheared off at the crop edge, so even the other party to it is not named. That is ONE reading, it is the ONLY thing in the corpus that names him, there is no directory line in any of the three volumes, no civic roll, no census, no trade and no street. The card's own present_on_scene_date reads `uncertain` for exactly this reason: the earliest source that names him is later than 1 July 1835. Two register rows of 27 June 1835, 160 acres, Residence UNKNOWN, against one press mention: a bare name on each side, which the rule refuses however close the dates fall. Refused, and the 160 acres come back off the card.

The MIDDLE INITIAL is on both sides, the town prints the middle name in full, and the man was the county's own recorder. The register holds exactly one Hamilton, spelled RICHARD J; the town holds Richard Jones Hamilton on the poll of 1833 ('Hamilton, R. J.'), the tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1834 ('Hamilton, Richard J.'), all three of them contemporary with the two school-section rows of 22 and 25 October 1833, and the printed record carries him forward without a break — three Democrat notices of 1834 ('Hon.', 'Col.'), Fergus 1839 'Hamilton, Rich'd J., clerk circuit court, Clark st cor. Randolph', Fergus 1843 'Hamilton, Richard Jones', Norris 1844, the 1840 census. He was clerk and recorder of Cook County from its organisation in 1831, which is to say the officer through whose hands land records passed. Upheld on the middle initial and the bracket together.

The KIMBALL WALTER shape: the man signs his own name, with the initial the register writes, in the town's own paper. The Chicago Democrat of 18 March 1834 carries a signed dissolution notice — 'The Co-partnership of Taylor & Handy was this day dissolved by mutual consent … H. S. HANDY, CHARLES TAYLOR. Chicago, Feb. 1, 1834' — which is a Chicago firm, a partner and a dated Chicago address over his signature, sixteen months before the register enters HANDY HENRY S for 240 acres on 27 June and 10 September 1835. Fergus's old-settler death notices hold him after, as 'Handy, Maj. Henry S.', printing the same middle initial a third time. Two independent town-side documents and the middle initial on both sides. It is the weakest uphold in the cohort and is marked so: there is no directory line, no civic roll and no Residence column, and the ruling rests on the signature and the death notice alone.

MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides, and the register's two spellings of this man mirror the town's own two habits. The town prints 'Harmon, C. L.' on the poll of 1834 and 'Chas. L. Harmon' on the 1837 election return; Fergus 1843 prints both a business card, 'C L. HARMON, commission merchant and wholesale grocer', and the roll entry 'Harmon, Charles Loomis, dry goods and groceries, 145 South Water'; Norris 1844's advertiser pages print 'C. L. Harmon'. The poll of 1834 falls between the two register rows. A wholesale grocer and dry-goods merchant taking a town lot at the school-section sale of 22 October 1833 for $130 is the trade the card already asserts doing what the card says it did. The register holds five Harmon spellings and the layer three Harmons, and the L is what separates this one from both Deweys.

Ruled with HARMON CHARLES L and it goes the same way, which is not the default — cohort C1's BROWN WM is what happens when a barer spelling is allowed to ride on a fuller one. It does not apply here because THIS SPELLING IS NOT BARER: CHAS L carries the middle initial, and the contraction 'Chas.' is precisely the form the 1837 election return and Norris 1844's advertiser card print for this man. The single row of 8 August 1835, 80.45 acres for $100.55, is upheld on the same middle initial and the same trade as the fuller spelling. Cohort A's abbreviated-and-full habit (HADDOCK E H / HADDOCK EDWARD H) is doing real work here rather than being assumed: the two spellings agree on the token that discriminates.

The MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides with the middle name printed in full behind it, and the Residence column reading COOK with a town-side partner to check it against. Fergus 1839 prints 'Harmon, Dr. Elijah D.' and Fergus 1843 'Harmon, Elijah Dewey, physician, bds C. L. Harmon [died January 3, 1869, aged 80]' — the whole middle name, the trade the card holds, and an age that puts birth about 1788, which agrees with Andreas's Bennington, Vermont, 20 August 1782 to within a printer's rounding of a death notice. The layer holds no second Elijah Harmon and the register no second Elijah. One of the two rows of 2 October 1834 states COOK, and cohort B's rule for that column — it needs a town-side partner — is met by the directories' printing of the same initial. Andreas has him pre-empting one hundred and forty acres with a northern boundary near Sixteenth Street, which is the same physician buying ground south of the town that the register's SWFR of section 22 is.

Ruled beside HARMON ISAAC D and it goes the OTHER way, which is the point of ruling paired spellings together. This row of 24 October 1833 prints the forename bare, with no middle initial, and the town's own printed record holds TWO Isaac Harmons: Fergus 1839's 'Harmon, Isaac D., dry goods merchant, 8 Clark street' and Fergus 1843's 'Harmon, Isaac Newton, with C. L. Harmon [died Nov. 8, 1891]'. The card's own crosswalk already records the collision — its evidence_against reads 'CONTESTED: 2 residents of 1835 meet this one entry on that rule, and at most one of them is the person printed'. The layer holds one Isaac Harmon because the layer is THIN, not because the town had one, which is BROWN WM exactly. The argument that would have upheld it — that a man 'with C. L. Harmon' in 1843 was likely too young to buy a $163 town lot in 1833 — is not taken, because Fergus prints his death and no age, and an unprinted age is a guess. Refused; the fuller spelling stands.

Cohort A's lesson run backwards and it holds: where the town's card carries only bare forenames, the DIRECTORY supplies the initial, and it is that printing which upholds. The card's own readings are all bare — 'HARMON, ISAAC' on the muster roll of 1832, 'Isaac Harmon' in the Democrat of 17 December 1833, 'Harmon, Isaac' in the Democrat of 5 August 1835 — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Harmon, Isaac D., dry goods merchant, 8 Clark street', which is the only place on the town's side the D appears. The register writes ISAAC D. The two Democrat printings bracket the row of 22 October 1833 on both sides, ten months before and twenty-one months after. A dry-goods merchant taking a town lot at the school-section sale for $130 is consistent with the trade. Upheld on the middle initial; the bare spelling two days later is refused above.

The PEARSONS pattern, and the largest carry in the cohort. The MIDDLE INITIAL K is on both sides and the town prints the name whole twice — Fergus 1839 'Hubbard, Elijah K., BANKER, 47-51 Dearborn st', and Fergus's death notices 'Hubbard, Elijah Kent', died 26 May 1839. The poll of 1835 holds him at Chicago in the same season as the entries, and the Democrat of 5 August 1835 and the American of 1835 print 'E. K. Hubbard' beside them. The twenty-four rows are one hand at work: twenty-three of them fall on 26 and 27 June 1835 and the last on 25 August, 2,428 acres for $3,509.82 — a banker buying at the ring in two afternoons is the trade the card holds doing what the card says it did, not a second Elijah K. Hubbard who happens to share the county and the week. The register's other Hubbards are GURDON S and THOMAS R, both discriminated by initial.

MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides, and no man of 1835 Chicago is held by more documents. The register writes GURDON S; the town prints 'G. S. Hubbard' in the Democrat of 1 April 1834, 'Gordon S. Hubbard' in the same paper of 13 August 1834 electing him a TOWN TRUSTEE, 'Col. G. S. Hubbard' in June 1835, 'Gurdon S. Hubbard' in the American of 4 July 1835, the poll of 1835, the 1840 census head 'Gurdon S. Hubbard', two Fergus 1843 business cards and the roll entry 'Hubbard, Gurdon Saltonstall, forwarding and commission, South Water', and Norris 1844. The single row of 22 October 1833 is 2.90 acres of the school section for $160 — ground inside the town, taken at the town's own sale by a packer and forwarding merchant whose premises were on South Water. The trustee notice of August 1834 is the same column that carries Ebenezer Goodrich, upheld above.

The fuller of a pair cohort A already read as one entry twice — it upheld HUNTER E E and named EDWARD E as the same row read with the Residence column on the fuller reading, so this is the reading that carries the column. MIDDLE INITIAL E on both sides; the town prints the forename whole on the poll of 1834 ('Hunter, Edward E.'), in the Democrat of 6 August 1834 ('Edward E. Hunter') and in Fergus's death notices ('Hunter, Edward E.'), and Fergus 1839 prints a trade and a street, 'Hunter, Edward [E.], deputy-sheriff, ex-justice of peace, Wells st'. One of the three rows of 15 November 1834 states COOK, and cohort B's requirement of a town-side partner for that column is met by the poll of 1834 three months earlier. Upheld.

`letter_list_only` at its plainest, and the directories make it worse rather than better. The card's own note: 'KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN — the Democrat of 22 October 1834 … a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further.' Cohort C1's warning was to read press_evidence[].list rather than the flag; read here, the flag is right and there is nothing else. Against that, the register prints SAMUEL bare on four rows of September and October 1833, and the printed record holds TWO Samuel Jacksons with middle names the register does not have — Fergus 1839 'Jackson, Samuel T., Government works, near Garrison', Fergus 1843 'Jackson, Samuel Thomas, overseer Chicago harbor' AND 'Jackson, Samuel Ezra, bds Samuel Jackson', both matched to this card as `ambiguous`. The county history's harbour foreman arriving from Buffalo in June 1833 is an enrichment of a name, not a check on a row: it predicts no purchase, and $328 of town lots that autumn is not what it predicts. Refused.

The town gave this man an OFFICE two weeks after the entries and he was advertising in its paper a month after them. Andreas: 'It was during these days that Benjamin Jones was appointed Street Commissioner' — 7 November 1833, the town's first — and the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries him as a paying advertiser, which the card calls strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833. The register's four rows are 22 and 24 October 1833, $1,133 of school-section town lots, a fortnight before the appointment. Fergus 1839 prints 'Jones, Benjamin, GROCER, South Water street' and Norris 1844 'Jones, Benjamin, of B. J. & Co.' with the firm's own card: a South Water grocer buying South Water ground at the town's own sale. The forename is printed in full on both sides, the layer holds one Benjamin Jones and the register discriminates its three Joneses by forename. Upheld on the bracket and the trade together.

Upheld on THREE contemporary civic rolls and an uncommon forename printed whole on both sides, and on nothing else — which is stated plainly because the directory evidence here is worthless. The town holds 'Jones, Willard' on the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834 and the poll of 1835; the tax list is the same year as the two school-section rows of 22 and 25 October 1833 and the polls hold him after, so the rolls bracket the entries on both sides. The layer holds exactly one Willard Jones and the register exactly one JONES WILLARD, where both records hold several plain Williams. The one directory line the crosswalk offers, Fergus 1839's 'Jones, Wm., justice of the peace', is matched `contested` between this man and William Jones and is not used: it cannot corroborate one of two claimants. Upheld on the second-document arm.

The block's BROWN WM, named as such by the ticket before the cohort was read, and the printed record is worse than Brown's. Fergus 1843 prints THREE distinct William Joneses — 'Jones, William [Golden]. (B. J. & Co.)', 'Jones, William Edwin (Ogden & J.)' and 'Jones, William Harrison, clerk, H. W. Bigelow' — and the 1839 line 'Jones, Wm., justice of the peace' is matched `contested` between this man and Willard Jones, who is upheld above. The register's three rows of 24 October 1833 and 5 August 1835 print WILLIAM bare, with no middle initial and UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and the four Democrat printings on the town's side are bare too ('Wm. Jones', 'Jones, Wm.'). The layer holds one William Jones on the commonest surname in the town because the layer is thin. A bare Wm. Jones on a tract row could be any of the three the directory prints or a fourth. Refused; 243.52 acres come back off the card.

retired.reasoning: GARRETT A ET CO is refused against A. Garrett — not because the firm is a stranger, but because the purchaser is a FIRM and this crosswalk proposes correspondences between a purchaser and a PERSON. 'ET CO' is the register saying the buyer was a partnership; the eighty acres in T38N R14E entered on 1 December 1835 were entered by the house, and a card that says this person entered them says something the page does not. The town's A. Garrett is well attested — an auctioneer in four numbers of the American and the Democrat — and the identification of the firm with him is probably right and is not what is refused. Reading firms as entities in their own right, so a partnership's purchase can be recorded against the partnership and its partners named, is T-0851.

So this judgement is now a derivation and a hand ruling on it would be a ruling on nothing — which is what --check called it. The reasoning is kept here rather than deleted: it is the argument the rule was written from, and the second firm the rule caught (PRUYNE P AND CO, whose entry had been written onto Peter Pruyne's card as his own) is what a hand ruling on one spelling could never reach.
